title: Local Perceptions Toward Large Carnivores in Zambia's East Musalangu Game Management Area: Implications for Conservation
content:
Local communities living adjacent to North Luangwa National Park in Zambia generally hold negative perceptions toward large carnivores, including lions, leopards, cheetahs, African wild dogs, and spotted hyenas, largely due to human–carnivore conflicts. Using semi-structured questionnaires, we found that education level, length of residence, and knowledge of carnivore species were the strongest predictors of attitudes, whereas livestock losses and demographic factors were not significant predictors. These findings highlight the importance of conservation education, community sensitisation, and support for stable livelihoods in fostering positive perceptions and improving coexistence between rural communities and large carnivores in protected area landscapes.


ABSTRACT

Human–carnivore conflict (HCC), encompassing livestock depredation, human injuries and fatalities, disease transmission, and retaliatory killings, represents a persistent and complex conservation challenge globally. Such interactions shape local perceptions with important implications for both community livelihoods and the long-term conservation of large carnivores. Using semi-structured questionnaires, we examined the relationship between community perceptions and key socio-demographic and economic characteristics among residents adjacent to North Luangwa National Park in northeastern Zambia. Overall, local residents exhibited predominantly negative perceptions toward the conservation of lions (Panthera leo), cheetahs (Acinonyx jubatus), leopards (Panthera pardus), African wild dogs (Lycaon pictus), and spotted hyenas (Crocuta crocuta). The main predictors of these perceptions were education level, length of residency, and knowledge of carnivore species, with higher education and greater familiarity associated with more favourable conservation attitudes. Other potential predictors, including gender, age, occupation, and the number of livestock owned or lost to carnivores, were not significantly associated with local perceptions. The results suggest that conservation education initiatives targeting communities with lower levels of formal education, and benefit-sharing mechanisms that make the economic value of large carnivores tangible to local residents, are critical to fostering tolerance and long-term coexistence with large carnivores in the East Musalangu Game Management Area.
